bull_thesis: The bull case is that the screening data on this company is simply out of date, and that a genuinely good business is being judged on its worst year. Ingles Markets is a family-controlled supermarket chain of roughly 195 stores across western North Carolina, upstate South Carolina, north Georgia and east Tennessee. Hurricane Helene struck its home market of Asheville in the last days of September 2024 -- the final days of its fiscal 2024. The damage shows up with unusual precision in the accounts: the quarter ended 2024-09-28 posted an operating loss of $1.4 million, and the quarter after it drained $88.8 million of working capital and burned $81.4 million of free cash. Fiscal 2025 was therefore a wrecked year, and every headline ratio built from it is wrong about the company today. The screening file reports a price-to-free-cash-flow multiple of 41 times; the actual trailing-twelve-month figure is 11.1 times. It reports earnings per share down 20.9%; the two most recent quarters are up 70% and up 60% year over year. It reports net debt of $177 million; the March 2026 balance sheet shows $112.5 million. It reports an insider sell ratio that looks like an exodus, but the 174,651 shares sold are almost entirely one family director, Laura Ingle Sharp, exiting her whole position between September 2023 and 2024-06-27, with no insider sale since -- and the only open-market trade of 2026 is a purchase, director Dwight L. Jacobs buying 500 shares at $88.07 on 2026-05-20. Underneath the noise sits a recovery that is real and accelerating. First-half fiscal 2026 net sales were $2.68 billion with net income of $52.4 million against $31.7 million a year earlier. Gross margin has expanded year over year for four consecutive quarters, reaching 24.87% in the March 2026 quarter against 23.36% a year before. Operating profit rose 66% and then 57.6% year over year in those two quarters. Cash has built from $353.7 million at the fiscal 2024 close to $418.0 million, and borrowings have been repaid every quarter. The balance sheet is close to unimpeachable: net debt of just 0.4 times cash operating profit, interest cover of 7.7 times, a current ratio of 3.3 times, an Altman-Z solvency score of 4.6, a Piotroski quality score of 7 of 9, no goodwill, no intangible assets, no stock-based compensation, and operating cash flow running at 2.46 times reported net income -- meaning the profits are backed by cash, not accounting entries. The debt is cheap and long-dated: $350 million of senior notes at 4.00% running to 2031 plus an undrawn $150 million facility to June 2030, which in a world of 4.5% ten-year yields is a small hidden asset. Then there is the property. The company owns the land and buildings under 174 of its supermarkets, the shopping centres several of those stores anchor, a fluid-dairy plant, and 29 undeveloped commercial sites. All of it is carried at heavily depreciated historical cost -- $1.53 billion net against a total market value of $1.67 billion. Milkco, the dairy plant, supplies about 65% of the milk sold in Ingles stores and ships 81% of its output to outside customers across 18 states, which makes it a real manufacturing business rather than a cost centre. And for the first time in the company history, an outside shareholder has a seat at the table: Summer Road LLC, holder of roughly 3% of the Class A shares, won the election of Rory A. Held to the board on 2026-04-30 with the support of about 62% of shares outstanding and roughly 70% of votes cast. Held disclosed 429,058 Class A shares held indirectly in a Form 3 on 2026-05-27. Institutions are following him in -- the March 2026 quarter filings show holders rising from 209 to 235 and shares held from 13.41 million to 14.23 million, with 52 brand-new positions against 26 closed. For this case to pay, three conditions must hold. The margin recovery has to be operating rather than mechanical. The three storm-closed stores have to reopen and contribute. bear_thesis: The bear case is not that this company is failing. At $87.94 the stock is up roughly 48% from its 52-week low of $59.27, sits 7% above its 200-day average, and is near the top of its one-year range against a high of $95.62. # Forensic Dossier — Ingles Markets, Incorporated (IMKTA)

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Price used:** $87.94 (US dollars, Nasdaq, live quote) · **Market value:** about $1.67 billion · **Shares:** 18.99 million (Class A and Class B combined)

**An unusual starting note.** Ingles has not held an earnings conference call since May 2016. The transcript archive for this company simply stops ten years ago. There is no guidance, no analyst question-and-answer session, and no management commentary beyond a single recycled sentence in each quarterly press release. This dossier therefore cross-examines the company's *actions and filings* rather than its words, because there are almost no words to examine. That absence is itself one of the most important findings here, and it is the reason an outside shareholder had to run a proxy contest in 2026 to win a board seat.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Because management does not narrate, the story has to be read off the income statement and the press releases. Across the last five fiscal years it breaks into three clean chapters.

**Chapter one — the pandemic windfall (fiscal 2021 through fiscal 2023).** Revenue climbed from $4.99 billion to $5.89 billion and profit exploded: earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA, a rough proxy for cash operating profit) peaked at $500.6 million in fiscal 2022, an 8.8% margin — roughly double what a regional supermarket normally earns. Per-share profit hit $14.36. Two forces did that work: households cooked at home, and food inflation let a grocer raise shelf prices faster than its own costs rose. Neither was repeatable, and management never claimed otherwise, because management never claimed anything.

**Chapter two — the give-back, then the storm (fiscal 2024 and 2025).** As food inflation cooled, the windfall reversed on schedule: EBITDA fell to $283.0 million in fiscal 2024 and $252.5 million in fiscal 2025, and per-share profit collapsed from $11.10 to $5.56 to $4.40. That quarter (ended 2024-09-28) posted an operating **loss** of $1.4 million and a small net loss. The following quarter drained $88.8 million of working capital and burned $81.4 million of free cash flow. The fiscal 2025 annual report records $9.0 million of cleanup and repair costs against $6.2 million of insurance recoveries, four stores closed, three of them still shut.

When pump prices fall, fuel shrinks as a share of the mix and the *blended* margin rises without a single operating improvement. Rough arithmetic suggests a quarter to a third of that 151-basis-point gain is this mix effect. The rest looks real — but anyone extrapolating the full improvement is extrapolating an oil price.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability score: not scoreable — and that is the finding.**

Ingles issues no guidance, so there is no promise to measure delivery against. Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions.

The favourable reading: a company that never guides can never be accused of managing to a number, and the cash-conversion evidence (operating cash flow at 2.46 times net income) says the reported profits are real. There is no sandbagging pattern because there is no bag.

The unfavourable reading: a shareholder buying this stock is underwriting an information vacuum. There is no way to know what management expects from the three storm-closed stores, what it thinks normalized fuel margins are, whether it intends to buy back stock, or how it values its own real estate. ## 5. Analyst pressure points

There are no analysts on a call to apply pressure, and the screening file notes there is no analyst price-target coverage for this listing. The pressure has instead arrived through the proxy machinery, and it concentrated on three subjects management has never voluntarily addressed:

1. **Capital allocation.** The company earns roughly $104 million a year, pays out only 11.8% of it as dividends (a yield of about 0.75%), buys back no stock, and lets cash accumulate. Cash has grown to $418 million — about 25% of the entire market value — earning deposit rates inside a business whose own return on invested capital is 4.7%. Summer Road's charge of poor capital deployment is arithmetically hard to dismiss.
2. **The real estate.** The company owns the property under 174 of its supermarkets, plus the shopping centres several of them anchor, plus a fluid-dairy plant, plus 29 undeveloped sites. All of it sits on the balance sheet at heavily depreciated historical cost — $1.53 billion net. Management has never publicly valued it. Outside estimates exist (a 2026-06-28 third-party research note argued for $110 to $120 per share on this basis), but the company itself is silent.
3. **Control and pay.** The dual-class structure — where the founding family's Class B shares carry ten votes each — means the family elects most of the board regardless of how the Class A shareholders vote. Class A holders elect a separate, small slate, and that is the only door Summer Road could walk through.

What worries outside holders that management is not addressing: whether any of the earnings recovery will ever be converted into a shareholder return, as opposed to a larger cash pile.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **A decade of silence.** No earnings call since May 2016; no guidance; a single boilerplate chairman quote per release (most recently 2026-05-07). For a listed company this is close to the disclosure floor.
- **Control the minority cannot outvote.** The 2026-04-30 annual meeting elected the activist's nominee to one seat — but the family's Class B slate (six directors, including the chairman and two other family members) was elected simultaneously and unopposed. One independent voice on a controlled board is a foot in the door, not a lever.
- **Returns below the cost of capital.** Return on invested capital of 4.7% and return on equity of 6.4% on the trailing twelve months. A business earning less than its capital costs creates no value by growing; it creates value only by shrinking, returning cash, or being revalued — and this one is doing none of the three on its own initiative.
- **The margin lift is partly an oil-price artifact.** As set out above, cheaper gasoline flatters the blended gross margin. Brent crude has risen roughly 24% since early July 2026 on the renewed Hormuz blockade. That tailwind is turning into a headwind inside the current quarter.
- **Cash trapped, not deployed.** $418 million of cash sitting against a 0.75% dividend and no buyback.

**Green flags**

- **A real, verified operating recovery.** Operating profit rose 66% year over year in the December 2025 quarter and 57.6% in the March 2026 quarter, on four straight quarters of gross-margin expansion.
- **A fortress balance sheet.** Net debt of $112.5 million against $279 million of EBITDA (0.4 times), interest cover of 7.7 times, current ratio 3.3 times, Altman-Z of 4.6. The debt is also cheap and long: $350 million of senior notes at 4.00% running to 2031, and an undrawn $150 million facility to June 2030. In a world of 4.5% ten-year yields, that is a small hidden asset.
- **Books without cosmetics.** No goodwill, no intangibles, no stock compensation, cash conversion of 2.46 times net income, inventory turning 8.5 times a year, a 34-day cash conversion cycle.
- **The insider tape is misread and is actually neutral-to-positive.** The only 2026 open-market transaction is a director's purchase of 500 shares at $88.07 on 2026-05-20 — a director paying essentially today's price with his own money.
- **Owned real estate and a genuine vertical asset.** Milkco, the company's dairy plant, supplies about 65% of the milk sold in Ingles stores and ships 81% of its output to outside customers across 18 states. That is a real manufacturing business hiding inside a grocer.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The activist's arithmetic is the loudest signal in the file.** Summer Road's chief investment officer Rory A. Held filed a Form 3 on 2026-05-27 disclosing 429,058 Class A shares held indirectly. That is real money committed before the seat was won, and it is a bet on capital allocation changing at a company that has never changed it.

In a company where the founding family controls the supermajority of voting power, a number that large means the family did not — or chose not to — block him in the Class A election. Read charitably, that is a controlling shareholder acknowledging the disclosure criticism. Read sceptically, it is the cheapest possible concession: one seat, no structural change.

There is no disclosure that tells you which, and that ambiguity matters more than any single quarter's earnings.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: STRENGTHENING — but off a storm-depressed base, and the market has already paid for most of it.**

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position is this: **every genuine positive here is already in the price.** The stock is $87.94 against a 52-week low of $59.27 — up roughly 48% from the trough — and sits 7% above its 200-day average near the top of its one-year range. Book value per share is $87.50, so the shares change hands at 1.01 times book. Trailing earnings of $5.49 per share put it on 15.7 times, at the upper end of where this company has historically traded. The operating recovery is real and the screening file's alarm about it is wrong; but being right about the recovery does not make the stock cheap, because the recovery is what the last twelve months of share-price gain already bought.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is scale-cost combined with local real-estate control: in the small towns of western North Carolina, upstate South Carolina, north Georgia and east Tennessee, Ingles frequently owns the best corner and the town is not large enough to support a second full-line supermarket. Vertical integration through Milkco adds a real cost edge on dairy. But the width test is the returns evidence, and the returns evidence is modest: return on invested capital of 4.7% and return on equity of 6.4% on the trailing twelve months, with a 2.7% operating margin. A genuinely wide moat shows up as returns comfortably above the cost of capital, sustained. These are not that.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Gross margin is expanding, not compressing — 24.5% on the trailing twelve months against 23.9% in fiscal 2025 and 23.0% in fiscal 2024 — and the company has not lost its markets. The multi-year decline from the 2022 peak is normalization from an anomaly, not erosion of a franchise. It would be wrong to grade this eroding on the strength of a comparison to a pandemic high-water mark.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, in the retail channel-shift family.** The structural force is real — Walmart, Aldi and warehouse clubs taking food share, and online grocery slowly changing the last mile. But Ingles' geography is the least exposed version of that risk: rural and small-town markets where hard-discount density is hard to build and delivery economics are poor, and where the company has already coexisted with Walmart for forty years. Revenue has grown, not shrunk, over five years — from $4.99 billion in fiscal 2021 to about $5.40 billion on the trailing twelve months. This is not a structurally shrinking base.

**So is the cheapness a mispricing or a trap?** Neither, which is the honest answer. It is not a value trap: the balance sheet is strong, the base is not melting, and the books are clean. But it is also no longer cheap. The mispricing that existed a year ago — a hurricane-depressed grocer at 0.7 times book with a misread insider file — has been substantially harvested by the market between the 52-week low and today. What remains is a fairly-priced, well-financed, slow-growing regional supermarket with a large pile of conservatively-carried real estate that a controlling family has shown no intention of monetizing. The real-estate value is genuine and it is genuinely unavailable. Size accordingly, and treat any purchase above roughly book value as paying full price for a business that earns less than its cost of capital.

# Forensic Dossier — Ingles Markets, Incorporated (IMKTA)

**Prepared:** 2026-07-27 · **Price used:** $87.94 (US dollars, Nasdaq, live quote) · **Market value:** about $1.67 billion · **Shares:** 18.99 million (Class A and Class B combined)

**An unusual starting note.** Ingles has not held an earnings conference call since May 2016. The transcript archive for this company simply stops ten years ago. There is no guidance, no analyst question-and-answer session, and no management commentary beyond a single recycled sentence in each quarterly press release. This dossier therefore cross-examines the company's *actions and filings* rather than its words, because there are almost no words to examine. That absence is itself one of the most important findings here, and it is the reason an outside shareholder had to run a proxy contest in 2026 to win a board seat.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Because management does not narrate, the story has to be read off the income statement and the press releases. Across the last five fiscal years it breaks into three clean chapters.

**Chapter one — the pandemic windfall (fiscal 2021 through fiscal 2023).** Revenue climbed from $4.99 billion to $5.89 billion and profit exploded: earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA, a rough proxy for cash operating profit) peaked at $500.6 million in fiscal 2022, an 8.8% margin — roughly double what a regional supermarket normally earns. Per-share profit hit $14.36. Two forces did that work: households cooked at home, and food inflation let a grocer raise shelf prices faster than its own costs rose. Neither was repeatable, and management never claimed otherwise, because management never claimed anything.

**Chapter two — the give-back, then the storm (fiscal 2024 and 2025).** As food inflation cooled, the windfall reversed on schedule: EBITDA fell to $283.0 million in fiscal 2024 and $252.5 million in fiscal 2025, and per-share profit collapsed from $11.10 to $5.56 to $4.40. Then Hurricane Helene struck western North Carolina at the very end of September 2024 — the last days of fiscal 2024. The company's home market is Asheville. That quarter (ended 2024-09-28) posted an operating **loss** of $1.4 million and a small net loss. The following quarter drained $88.8 million of working capital and burned $81.4 million of free cash flow. The fiscal 2025 annual report records $9.0 million of cleanup and repair costs against $6.2 million of insurance recoveries, four stores closed, three of them still shut.

**Chapter three — the recovery now underway (fiscal 2026 so far).** This is the chapter the screening data has not caught up with. The first half of fiscal 2026 delivered net sales of $2.68 billion and net income of $52.4 million against $31.7 million a year earlier. Per-share profit in the December 2025 quarter rose 70% year over year and in the March 2026 quarter rose 60%. Cash on the balance sheet has climbed from $353.7 million (fiscal 2024 year-end) to $418.0 million. Debt has been paid down every single quarter.

**What was quietly dropped:** nothing, because nothing was ever promised. **What was quietly added:** an activist shareholder. In April 2026, Summer Road LLC — holder of roughly 3% of the Class A shares — took the company to a contested vote and won.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

Management makes essentially one claim per quarter. From the 2026-05-07 second-quarter release, Chairman Robert P. Ingle II said the results "are made possible by our associates' commitment and dedication to our customers and communities in which we serve." That is the entire narrative. It is not falsifiable, and it is repeated in substantially identical form quarter after quarter.

So the more useful forensic exercise is to test the *screening file's* claims — the numbers a portfolio director would otherwise act on — against the current financial reality. Several of them are badly stale, and the errors all run in the same direction.

| Claim in the screening file | What the current filings show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Price to free cash flow 41.2 times" | 11.1 times on the trailing twelve months ($151.3 million of free cash flow). The 41-times figure divides today's price by fiscal 2025's storm-depressed $39.7 million | **Wrong by roughly four times.** A hurricane artifact |
| "Earnings per share down 20.9% year over year" | Down 20.9% for *fiscal 2025*. The two most recent quarters are **up 70% and up 60%** year over year | **Stale by two quarters and directionally inverted** |
| "Revenue down 5.4%" | Fiscal-year figure. The December 2025 quarter grew 6.6% year over year; the March 2026 quarter fell 1.8%, almost entirely on cheaper gasoline | **Misleading** |
| "Free cash flow margin 0.7%" | 2.8% on the trailing twelve months; the fiscal 2025 figure was crushed by a one-off $88.8 million working-capital drain in the post-storm quarter | **Artifact** |
| "Net debt $177 million" | $112.5 million as of 2026-03-28 ($504 million of borrowings plus $26.7 million of capitalized leases, less $418.0 million of cash) | **Corrected downward** |
| "Insider buy ratio 0.01" — i.e. heavy selling | The 174,651 shares sold are almost entirely **one person**: family director Laura Ingle Sharp, who sold her whole position down to zero between September 2023 and 2024-06-27. There has been no insider sale since. The only 2026 open-market trade is a **purchase** — director Dwight L. Jacobs bought 500 shares at $88.07 on 2026-05-20 | **Materially misread.** A two-year-old estate-style exit, not live pessimism |
| "Margin 1.24 standard deviations below its historical peak" | True, and correct — but the "peak" is the 2022 pandemic anomaly. Measuring against it makes normality look like distress | **True but useless** |

Where the story is *poorer* than the numbers: management's silence gives no credit for a genuinely strong balance sheet. Interest cover is 7.7 times, net debt is 0.4 times EBITDA, the current ratio is 3.3 times, the Altman-Z solvency score is 4.6, and the Piotroski quality score is 7 of 9. Cash flow from operations runs at 2.46 times reported net income — an unusually high ratio that means the earnings are backed by real cash, not accruals. There is no goodwill, no intangible assets and no stock-based compensation anywhere on the statements. This is an exceptionally clean set of books.

Where the story is *richer* than the numbers: the gross margin improvement is partly mechanical. Gross margin rose to 24.87% in the March 2026 quarter from 23.36% a year before. But gasoline is roughly 12% of sales at a margin of only about 6%, versus roughly 27% in the rest of the store. When pump prices fall, fuel shrinks as a share of the mix and the *blended* margin rises without a single operating improvement. Rough arithmetic suggests a quarter to a third of that 151-basis-point gain is this mix effect. The rest looks real — but anyone extrapolating the full improvement is extrapolating an oil price.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rating: not assessable from management; strengthening from the numbers.**

There is no tone to trace. The company has issued no forward guidance in a decade and holds no calls. The chairman's quoted sentence in the 2026-05-07 release is the same sentiment as prior releases, carrying no information about demand, cost, competition or capital plans.

The only party actually speaking about this business with specificity is the activist. In its April 2026 proxy materials Summer Road used dated, pointed language: "disastrous capital allocation," "outsized compensation for Chairman and controlling shareholder Robert P. Ingle, II," and "deficient disclosure." The company's response was to campaign against Summer Road's nominee on conflict-of-interest grounds rather than to rebut the disclosure charge.

What the financial record shows, quarter by quarter, is a defensive posture converting into an improving one: four consecutive quarters of year-over-year gross margin expansion, cash building, debt shrinking, and capital spending stepped down from $114.5 million in fiscal 2025 to a $53.0 million first-half pace in fiscal 2026. That is a company husbanding cash after a shock, not investing into growth.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Reliability score: not scoreable — and that is the finding.**

Ingles issues no guidance, so there is no promise to measure delivery against. Two things follow, and they point in opposite directions.

The favourable reading: a company that never guides can never be accused of managing to a number, and the cash-conversion evidence (operating cash flow at 2.46 times net income) says the reported profits are real. There is no sandbagging pattern because there is no bag.

The unfavourable reading: a shareholder buying this stock is underwriting an information vacuum. There is no way to know what management expects from the three storm-closed stores, what it thinks normalized fuel margins are, whether it intends to buy back stock, or how it values its own real estate. The market has to infer everything from a quarterly press release and an annual report. That is a genuine and permanent discount factor, not a temporary one — and it is precisely what the activist campaigned on.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

There are no analysts on a call to apply pressure, and the screening file notes there is no analyst price-target coverage for this listing. The pressure has instead arrived through the proxy machinery, and it concentrated on three subjects management has never voluntarily addressed:

1. **Capital allocation.** The company earns roughly $104 million a year, pays out only 11.8% of it as dividends (a yield of about 0.75%), buys back no stock, and lets cash accumulate. Cash has grown to $418 million — about 25% of the entire market value — earning deposit rates inside a business whose own return on invested capital is 4.7%. Summer Road's charge of poor capital deployment is arithmetically hard to dismiss.
2. **The real estate.** The company owns the property under 174 of its supermarkets, plus the shopping centres several of them anchor, plus a fluid-dairy plant, plus 29 undeveloped sites. All of it sits on the balance sheet at heavily depreciated historical cost — $1.53 billion net. Management has never publicly valued it. Outside estimates exist (a 2026-06-28 third-party research note argued for $110 to $120 per share on this basis), but the company itself is silent.
3. **Control and pay.** The dual-class structure — where the founding family's Class B shares carry ten votes each — means the family elects most of the board regardless of how the Class A shareholders vote. Class A holders elect a separate, small slate, and that is the only door Summer Road could walk through.

What worries outside holders that management is not addressing: whether any of the earnings recovery will ever be converted into a shareholder return, as opposed to a larger cash pile.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

**Red flags**

- **A decade of silence.** No earnings call since May 2016; no guidance; a single boilerplate chairman quote per release (most recently 2026-05-07). For a listed company this is close to the disclosure floor.
- **Control the minority cannot outvote.** The 2026-04-30 annual meeting elected the activist's nominee to one seat — but the family's Class B slate (six directors, including the chairman and two other family members) was elected simultaneously and unopposed. One independent voice on a controlled board is a foot in the door, not a lever.
- **Returns below the cost of capital.** Return on invested capital of 4.7% and return on equity of 6.4% on the trailing twelve months. A business earning less than its capital costs creates no value by growing; it creates value only by shrinking, returning cash, or being revalued — and this one is doing none of the three on its own initiative.
- **The margin lift is partly an oil-price artifact.** As set out above, cheaper gasoline flatters the blended gross margin. Brent crude has risen roughly 24% since early July 2026 on the renewed Hormuz blockade. That tailwind is turning into a headwind inside the current quarter.
- **Cash trapped, not deployed.** $418 million of cash sitting against a 0.75% dividend and no buyback.

**Green flags**

- **A real, verified operating recovery.** Operating profit rose 66% year over year in the December 2025 quarter and 57.6% in the March 2026 quarter, on four straight quarters of gross-margin expansion.
- **A fortress balance sheet.** Net debt of $112.5 million against $279 million of EBITDA (0.4 times), interest cover of 7.7 times, current ratio 3.3 times, Altman-Z of 4.6. The debt is also cheap and long: $350 million of senior notes at 4.00% running to 2031, and an undrawn $150 million facility to June 2030. In a world of 4.5% ten-year yields, that is a small hidden asset.
- **Books without cosmetics.** No goodwill, no intangibles, no stock compensation, cash conversion of 2.46 times net income, inventory turning 8.5 times a year, a 34-day cash conversion cycle.
- **The insider tape is misread and is actually neutral-to-positive.** The only 2026 open-market transaction is a director's purchase of 500 shares at $88.07 on 2026-05-20 — a director paying essentially today's price with his own money.
- **Owned real estate and a genuine vertical asset.** Milkco, the company's dairy plant, supplies about 65% of the milk sold in Ingles stores and ships 81% of its output to outside customers across 18 states. That is a real manufacturing business hiding inside a grocer.
- **Institutions are accumulating, not fleeing.** The 13F records for the March 2026 quarter show holders rising from 209 to 235, shares held from 13.41 million to 14.23 million, with 52 brand-new positions against 26 closed.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The activist's arithmetic is the loudest signal in the file.** Summer Road's chief investment officer Rory A. Held filed a Form 3 on 2026-05-27 disclosing 429,058 Class A shares held indirectly. That is real money committed before the seat was won, and it is a bet on capital allocation changing at a company that has never changed it.

**The 62% vote is more interesting than the seat.** Held was elected with the support of roughly 62% of shares outstanding and about 70% of votes cast. In a company where the founding family controls the supermajority of voting power, a number that large means the family did not — or chose not to — block him in the Class A election. Read charitably, that is a controlling shareholder acknowledging the disclosure criticism. Read sceptically, it is the cheapest possible concession: one seat, no structural change.

**The board is being quietly refreshed.** Three new directors have appeared in eight months: Larry Keith Collins (Form 3, 2025-12-01), and Dwight L. Jacobs and Rory A. Held (both effective 2026-04-30). One of them bought stock in the open market within three weeks of joining. New voices on a board that has been static for years is a change in the machinery, even if the votes still sit with the family.

**The capital-spending step-down is a decision no one announced.** Capital expenditure ran $114.5 million in fiscal 2025 against $122.9 million of depreciation; the fiscal 2026 first half ran at $53.0 million. Spending below depreciation in a store-based retailer is either prudent post-storm discipline or the beginning of under-investment in the estate. There is no disclosure that tells you which, and that ambiguity matters more than any single quarter's earnings.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: STRENGTHENING — but off a storm-depressed base, and the market has already paid for most of it.**

The single most important thing the director must weigh before sizing a position is this: **every genuine positive here is already in the price.** The stock is $87.94 against a 52-week low of $59.27 — up roughly 48% from the trough — and sits 7% above its 200-day average near the top of its one-year range. Book value per share is $87.50, so the shares change hands at 1.01 times book. Trailing earnings of $5.49 per share put it on 15.7 times, at the upper end of where this company has historically traded. The operating recovery is real and the screening file's alarm about it is wrong; but being right about the recovery does not make the stock cheap, because the recovery is what the last twelve months of share-price gain already bought.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** The moat type is scale-cost combined with local real-estate control: in the small towns of western North Carolina, upstate South Carolina, north Georgia and east Tennessee, Ingles frequently owns the best corner and the town is not large enough to support a second full-line supermarket. Vertical integration through Milkco adds a real cost edge on dairy. But the width test is the returns evidence, and the returns evidence is modest: return on invested capital of 4.7% and return on equity of 6.4% on the trailing twelve months, with a 2.7% operating margin. A genuinely wide moat shows up as returns comfortably above the cost of capital, sustained. These are not that.

**Moat trend: STABLE.** Gross margin is expanding, not compressing — 24.5% on the trailing twelve months against 23.9% in fiscal 2025 and 23.0% in fiscal 2024 — and the company has not lost its markets. The multi-year decline from the 2022 peak is normalization from an anomaly, not erosion of a franchise. It would be wrong to grade this eroding on the strength of a comparison to a pandemic high-water mark.

**Secular threat: MANAGEABLE, in the retail channel-shift family.** The structural force is real — Walmart, Aldi and warehouse clubs taking food share, and online grocery slowly changing the last mile. But Ingles' geography is the least exposed version of that risk: rural and small-town markets where hard-discount density is hard to build and delivery economics are poor, and where the company has already coexisted with Walmart for forty years. Revenue has grown, not shrunk, over five years — from $4.99 billion in fiscal 2021 to about $5.40 billion on the trailing twelve months. This is not a structurally shrinking base.

**So is the cheapness a mispricing or a trap?** Neither, which is the honest answer. It is not a value trap: the balance sheet is strong, the base is not melting, and the books are clean. But it is also no longer cheap. The mispricing that existed a year ago — a hurricane-depressed grocer at 0.7 times book with a misread insider file — has been substantially harvested by the market between the 52-week low and today. What remains is a fairly-priced, well-financed, slow-growing regional supermarket with a large pile of conservatively-carried real estate that a controlling family has shown no intention of monetizing. The real-estate value is genuine and it is genuinely unavailable. Size accordingly, and treat any purchase above roughly book value as paying full price for a business that earns less than its cost of capital.

CREDIBILITY_SCORE: 3 | TRAJECTORY: STRENGTHENING | MOAT: NARROW | MOAT_TREND: STABLE | SECULAR_THREAT: manageable
